analysis.one_liner: Restores EPA authority to require water pollution permits for stormwater runoff from oil, gas, and mining sites.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a House subcommittee, with 39 Democrats signed on, no Republicans, and no vote in either chamber before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently bars the EPA from requiring oil, gas, and mining operations to get a Clean Water Act permit for runoff of collected stormwater from their sites. This bill removes that exemption, so those operations could be required to get a pollution permit, and directs the Interior Department to study how stormwater from oil and gas sites contaminates groundwater and aquifers.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near oil, gas, and mining operations — especially in fracking regions like northeastern Pennsylvania — whose drinking water, wells, and streams are exposed to contaminated runoff. The bill would let the EPA require discharge permits, and the new Interior Department study would document measurable contamination and aquifer susceptibility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near oil and gas sites

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the provision of the Clean Water Act that prohibits the EPA from requiring a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit for collected, uncontaminated stormwater runoff from mining and oil and gas operations, restoring the agency's authority to regulate those discharges.

Requires the Secretary of the Interior to study stormwater impacts in areas that may be contaminated by runoff from oil or gas operations, analyzing measurable contamination, groundwater resources, and the susceptibility of aquifers to contamination, with a report to Congress within one year.

Stormwater that collects on well pads and mining sites can carry pollutants into streams and groundwater; the bill closes a gap that has kept those discharges outside Clean Water Act permitting since 2005.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies and mining operators, who would face the cost of applying for discharge permits and managing stormwater to avoid illegal discharges. Some of those compliance costs could be passed to consumers or affect drilling economics in producing regions.

drawbacks.text: Requiring permits for stormwater discharges would add compliance costs and paperwork for oil, gas, and mining operators, which supporters of the exemption argue falls hardest on smaller producers and could slow domestic energy production.

The bill regulates only collected stormwater that the site itself would classify as uncontaminated; it does not directly address other pollution pathways from fracking, so its practical impact depends on how aggressively the EPA chooses to use the restored authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is protection of drinking water and streams in communities that host drilling and mining, at a cost borne mainly by the operators in the form of permit compliance. The bill is narrow — it restores a permitting authority and funds a study rather than imposing new performance standards — so its real-world impact depends on subsequent EPA action. Still, the cost falls on the industry creating the runoff rather than on taxpayers or residents.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee on the day after introduction, and it never received a markup, floor vote, or Senate action before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on March 23, 2021, with 35 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and then to its Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where action ended.
The bill accumulated 39 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a committee markup or a floor vote in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas and mining operators are better off: the Clean Water Act exemption for their stormwater runoff remains in place, and they avoid permit costs that the bill would have exposed them to. Communities near drilling and mining sites get no new protection.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.role: U.S. Representative, Pennsylvania's 8th District; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FRESHER Act and recruited 35 original cosponsors; his district includes fracking-affected communities in northeastern Pennsylvania.

for.name: 39 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-of-caucus Democratic support but no Republican cosponsor.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or brought it to the floor during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Beneficiary of the existing Clean Water Act stormwater exemption
against.what_they_did: The existing exemption the bill would repeal dates to 2005 energy legislation; the industry favors keeping stormwater runoff from drilling sites outside NPDES permitting. No industry group's opposition to this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill died in committee without any recorded vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Oil and gas operators, including fracking companies
industries.note: The bill repeals their exemption from Clean Water Act stormwater permits, exposing runoff discharges at well pads to NPDES permitting. Their cost of avoiding that regulation is the bill's entire purpose; residents near drilling sites bear the runoff instead.
The bill also removes the exemption for collected stormwater runoff from mining operations, subjecting those discharges to the same permitting authority.
